title: The Mambilla hydroelectric project
subtitle: Fifty years, four contractors, and not one kilowatt.
summary: Nigeria has pursued a 3,050 MW hydroelectric scheme on the Mambilla Plateau since a 1972 feasibility study, awarding and rescinding contracts in 2003, 2007, 2009, 2012 and 2017 amid corruption findings and international arbitration. Surveyors abandoned the site in June 2022 over two years of non-payment, and the project has generated no electricity.
lesson: Re-awarding a contract is not progress; it resets the clock while the need it was meant to serve compounds.
locationRole: Dam site on the Donga River

title: The Lagos Metropolitan Rail
subtitle: Flagged off with a ceremony. Cancelled eighteen months later, nothing built.
summary: Governor Lateef Jakande launched a 28.5-kilometre elevated line from Marina to Agege in July 1983, contracted at N689 million to a nineteen-firm French consortium and designed for 88,000 passengers an hour across 19 stations. Buhari's incoming military government terminated it in January 1985, writing off about $78 million with no piling, corridor or rolling stock to show, and Lagos waited until September 2023 for its first light rail line.
lesson: A project owned by one administration is a liability the next one can cash in; anchor it in something harder than political patronage.
locationRole: Planned rail corridor from Marina to Agege

title: The Old Federal Secretariat
subtitle: Fifteen storeys on the most expensive land in Lagos, and nobody inside it.
summary: Built in 1976 across roughly 120,000 square metres of Ikoyi, the Secretariat housed Nigeria's federal civil service until the capital moved to Abuja in December 1991 and it emptied overnight. A 2006 concession to convert it into 480 flats collapsed when Lagos State refused residential zoning, and the building still stands derelict with foregone rent estimated at about N93.5 billion.
lesson: Decide the second use of a public asset before its first use ends; a building nobody owns the decision on simply rots where it stands.
